headwords.definition: money received regularly from work, business, or other sources
examples: Her monthly income changes because she works freelance.
The family lost part of its income when the shop closed temporarily.

headwords.definition: money spent on a particular need, service, or activity
examples: Rent is my largest monthly expense.
I recorded the repair as an unexpected expense.

headwords.definition: completely necessary rather than optional
examples: Medicine is an essential expense, while a new phone can wait.
The budget protects essential services before entertainment.

headwords.definition: not necessary for basic needs or an important purpose
examples: I reduced nonessential spending for two months before the trip.
A café visit is nonessential, but small pleasures still need a realistic place in a budget.

headwords.definition: an expense that usually stays similar each period
examples: Rent is a fixed cost, so I plan for it before flexible spending.
The business lowered its fixed costs by moving to a smaller office.

headwords.definition: an expense whose amount changes according to use or circumstances
examples: Electricity is a variable cost because heating use changes by season.
Food is necessary, but its variable cost can still be managed.

headwords.definition: to have enough money for something without causing unacceptable difficulty
examples: I can afford the course if I save part of two paychecks.
A low price does not help if the buyer cannot afford the ongoing fees.

headwords.definition: the amount needed for housing, food, transport, and ordinary life in a place
examples: The salary looked high until I compared the city's cost of living.
Rising rent has increased the cost of living for students.

headwords.definition: the movement of money into and out of a person, household, or business
examples: A yearly fee created a cash-flow problem even though the annual budget was balanced.
Freelancers need to manage cash flow during months when clients pay late.

headwords.definition: money remaining after necessary costs and taxes
examples: She uses part of her disposable income for books and travel.
Higher transport costs left the household with less disposable income.

headwords.definition: stress caused by difficulty meeting money needs or obligations
examples: Unexpected medical costs placed the family under financial pressure.
Sharing housing reduced some financial pressure during university.

headwords.definition: to have just enough money to pay necessary expenses
examples: He worked extra weekend shifts to make ends meet.
Families may struggle to make ends meet when food prices rise quickly.

headwords.definition: a plan for how income will be used during a period
examples: My monthly budget includes a small amount for unexpected costs.

headwords.definition: to plan how much money can be used for different purposes
examples: I budget for annual insurance by saving a little each month.

headwords.definition: to assign money to a particular purpose
examples: We allocate part of every paycheck to rent and savings.

headwords.definition: a group of similar expenses used to organize a budget
examples: I created a separate category for transport and fuel.

headwords.definition: the maximum amount allowed for spending
examples: I set a weekly limit for restaurant meals.

headwords.definition: to spend more than planned or more than can be afforded
examples: I tend to overspend when I shop without a list.

headwords.definition: to spend less than the planned amount
examples: We underspent on transport because we walked more often.

headwords.definition: happening or calculated once each week
examples: A weekly budget works well for groceries and small personal costs.
I make a weekly transfer to my savings account.

headwords.definition: happening or calculated once each month
examples: A monthly plan matches the way my salary and rent are paid.
Monthly totals hide the fact that I spent too much in one weekend.

headwords.definition: based on what is genuinely possible rather than an ideal wish
examples: A realistic budget includes occasional social activities.
Saving half my income would not be realistic while I pay high rent.

headwords.definition: to change a plan slightly when circumstances change
examples: I adjusted the food budget after prices increased.
The plan needs to be adjusted when income falls unexpectedly.

headwords.definition: to record and follow money over time
examples: I track every card payment for one month when spending feels unclear.

headwords.definition: stored information showing a financial action or history
examples: The bank record showed that the payment had been made twice.

headwords.definition: to write down or electronically store financial information

headwords.definition: an official list of activity in a bank account over a period

headwords.definition: the amount of money currently available or owed in an account
examples: I check my balance before making a large purchase.
The account balance fell below the minimum after the fee was charged.

headwords.definition: a digital table used to organize and calculate financial information
examples: My spreadsheet automatically totals each spending category.
A simple spreadsheet gives me more control than a complicated app.

headwords.definition: an official document summarizing financial activity or an amount due
examples: The credit-card statement listed the payment deadline clearly.
I downloaded the statement before closing the account.

headwords.definition: to examine financial information carefully in order to assess it
examples: I review my spending every Sunday evening.
We reviewed three months of bills before changing the budget.

sections.title: Saving, Emergency Funds, and Short-Term Goals

headwords.definition: to keep money instead of spending it now
examples: I save a fixed amount as soon as my salary arrives.
She saved for six months before replacing her laptop.

headwords.definition: money kept for future use rather than current spending
examples: My savings covered the repair without using a credit card.
She keeps travel savings separate from her emergency money.

headwords.definition: money reserved for urgent, unexpected, and necessary costs
examples: The emergency fund paid for a dental problem between paychecks.
I rebuilt my emergency fund after using it for car repairs.

headwords.definition: extra money that protects against unexpected costs or income loss
examples: A small financial cushion made the job change less frightening.
Freelancers need a larger cushion because payments may arrive late.

headwords.definition: a specific result someone plans to achieve
examples: My first financial goal is to repay the small loan.
A clear goal makes it easier to refuse an unnecessary purchase.

headwords.definition: a specific amount or result to aim for
examples: I set a savings target based on the actual cost of the course.
The original target became unrealistic after rent increased.

headwords.definition: a scheduled electronic movement of money between accounts
examples: An automatic transfer moves money to savings on payday.
I lowered the transfer temporarily when my working hours changed.

headwords.definition: to reserve money for a particular future purpose
examples: We set aside part of the refund for winter heating.
I set money aside before spending on entertainment.

headwords.definition: informal savings kept for unexpected difficulty
examples: Their rainy-day fund covered two weeks without income.
A rainy-day fund should be easy to access but not mixed with daily spending.

headwords.definition: an important stage showing progress toward a larger goal
examples: Saving the first month's expenses was an encouraging milestone.
We celebrated the debt-repayment milestone without spending heavily.

phrases.text: I save first instead of waiting to see what remains.

A specific target makes progress easier to measure.
I keep different goals in separate accounts.

headwords.definition: an organized approach to present money needs and future goals
examples: Our financial plan includes debt repayment, savings, and retirement contributions.
The plan changed after the family decided to move.

headwords.definition: a condition in which finances are reliable enough to handle normal needs and changes
examples: A steady income gave the household greater financial stability.
Stability does not require wealth, but it does require some room for problems.

headwords.definition: protected from serious financial risk or uncertainty
examples: She felt more secure after building three months of basic expenses.
A permanent job does not make every household financially secure.

headwords.definition: continuing or planned over many years
examples: A long-term goal may require small actions across decades.
The cheap repair solved today's problem but increased long-term costs.

headwords.definition: the period after a person permanently stops regular paid work
examples: He began saving for retirement with his first full-time job.
Retirement planning is harder for workers with irregular income.

headwords.definition: regular income or a fund intended to support someone after retirement
examples: Her employer contributes to a workplace pension.
The pension alone may not cover future housing costs.

headwords.definition: to prepare something to remain useful despite future changes
examples: Learning new skills can help future-proof a person's income.
The family tried to future-proof its plan against higher energy costs.

headwords.definition: a possible future problem for which a plan or money is prepared
examples: The project budget includes a contingency for material price increases.
Illness is one contingency that a self-employed worker must consider.

Starting early reduces the amount required later.
The goal is security rather than a perfect prediction.

phrases.text: Future costs are uncertain, so the plan needs some flexibility.

headwords.definition: an arrangement with a bank for holding and managing money
examples: I keep bill money in a separate current account.
The bank froze the account after detecting unusual activity.

headwords.definition: to put money into a bank account
examples: I deposited the cash before the rent payment was due.
The employer deposits salaries directly into staff accounts.

headwords.definition: to take money out of a bank account
examples: She withdrew enough cash for the weekend market.

headwords.definition: to move money electronically from one account or person to another

headwords.definition: money given to pay for goods, services, or debt

headwords.definition: money charged for a service or permission

headwords.definition: money paid for borrowing or earned by saving
examples: The loan's interest adds considerably to the total cost.
This savings account pays a small amount of interest each month.

headwords.definition: banking services accessed through a website or app
examples: Online banking lets me schedule bills without visiting a branch.

headwords.definition: a phone or online service that stores payment methods electronically
examples: My digital wallet lets me pay without carrying the physical card.
A lost phone is less dangerous when the wallet uses strong security.

headwords.definition: allowing payment by holding a card or device near a reader
examples: Contactless payment is convenient for small transport fares.
I disabled contactless features after losing the card.

headwords.definition: criminal deception intended to obtain money or financial information

Education can help older customers recognize online fraud attempts.

headwords.definition: to protect money, accounts, or information from risk
examples: A password manager helps secure financial accounts.

headwords.definition: money that a person or organization owes
examples: She paid off the small debt before applying for another loan.
High-interest debt can grow even when regular payments are made.

headwords.definition: to receive money temporarily with an agreement to return it
examples: I would borrow only the amount needed for tuition.
The business borrowed money to replace unsafe equipment.

headwords.definition: money lent with an agreement about repayment, often including interest
examples: The student loan covered fees but not all living costs.
I compared the total loan cost rather than only the monthly payment.

headwords.definition: to return borrowed money
examples: He repays the loan automatically on payday.
The family needed more time to repay the emergency borrowing.

headwords.definition: one of several regular payments used to repay a total amount
examples: The final installment is due in September.
A low installment can hide a very long and expensive loan.

headwords.definition: an arrangement allowing someone to receive goods or money now and pay later
examples: Easy credit encouraged him to replace a phone that still worked.
The shop offered six months of interest-free credit.

headwords.definition: a card that lets the user borrow for purchases up to an agreed limit
examples: I pay the credit-card balance in full whenever possible.
The credit card was useful for the emergency repair, but the interest was high.

headwords.definition: requiring no interest payment for a stated period
examples: The interest-free offer is useful only if the full amount is repaid on time.
Her parents provided an interest-free loan for the course.

headwords.definition: to fail to make an agreed debt payment

headwords.definition: to put money into an asset or activity with the aim of future growth or income
examples: She invests a small regular amount rather than trying to predict the market.

headwords.definition: money or resources placed somewhere for future benefit
examples: Every investment carries some possibility of loss.

headwords.definition: money gained or lost from an investment

headwords.definition: the possibility of financial loss or an unfavorable result

headwords.definition: to spread money across different assets or sources to reduce dependence on one

headwords.definition: the collection of investments owned by a person or organization

headwords.definition: to grow through returns being added and producing further returns

headwords.definition: a general rise in prices that reduces what money can buy

headwords.definition: valuable money, property, and assets owned beyond immediate income

headwords.definition: something valuable that a person or organization owns

sections.title: Financial Tools, Apps, and Professional Advice

headwords.definition: software designed to record spending and support money planning
examples: The budgeting app groups card payments automatically.

headwords.definition: a resource, calculation, or service used to understand or manage money
examples: A loan calculator is a simple financial tool with a clear purpose.
Online tools can compare scenarios without making the decision for you.

headwords.definition: an automatic message from an app or service
examples: A notification warns me when the account balance is low.

headwords.definition: to make a financial action happen automatically through a system
examples: I automate regular bill payments but still review the amounts.

headwords.definition: control over who can access personal and financial information

headwords.definition: money earned for selling or arranging a financial product

headwords.definition: a screen that summarizes financial information in one place
